title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination

paper.title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination
paper.abstract:
Abstract In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse.
Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs’ ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen , a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment.
We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator’s worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity.
Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen .

PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination Paul Teiletche Affiliation: EPFL Affiliation: UC Berkeley Kanghyun Ryu Affiliation: UC Berkeley Kyungjoon Park Affiliation: Yonsei University Dhruva Tirumala Affiliation: Google DeepMind Markus Wulfmeier Affiliation: Nomagic * Equal contribution Negar Mehr Affiliation: UC Berkeley Abstract In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs’ ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen , a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment. We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator’s worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity. Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen . 1 Introduction Figure 1: Overview of PopGen . Left (Stage 1): An LLM produces a diverse set of behaviors at the text level using oversampling. Right (Stage 2): Each behavior description enters an iterative refinement loop: a generator translates the behavior into an executable policy (Policy Code), which is evaluated with a VLM through environment rollouts. An advisor then analyzes rollout results and provides feedback to guide subsequent refinement attempts. Training agents that collaborate effectively with unseen partners is a key challenge in multi-agent systems like robotics or cooperative video games. The task, known as zero-shot coordination (ZSC), requires a cooperator to coordinate with partners it has never interacted with, whose conventions, skill level, and strategy are unknown at test time. This problem is challenging because cooperative tasks typically admit many equally effective but mutually incompatible conventions, so a cooperator trained with one arbitrary convention may fail when paired with a partner that follows a different one ( Hu et al., 2020 ; Carroll et al., 2019 ) . A common approach to ZSC is population play, which trains a cooperator against a population of partner agents. The effectiveness of population play depends on the diversity of the population against which the cooperator is trained, since a high coverage of the strategy space during training increases the likelihood that the test-time partner is in-distribution for the cooperator, allowing them to collaborate effectively ( Strouse et al., 2021 ; Lupu et al., 2021 ; Sarkar et al., 2023 ) . Existing methods build such populations by optimizing diversity proxies computed from trajectory statistics ( Lupu et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . However, these measures may fail to capture what humans perceive as meaningfully distinct strategies ( Bettini et al., 2024c ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . For example, two chefs may take different trajectories in a kitchen while following the same strategy (e.g., only carrying onions). The issue is not that these trajectories are wrongly classified as different (they are indeed different), but that optimizing for such diversity can lead to undesired training populations that are diverse in their motion but do not cover the distinct strategies that matter for coordination ( Sarkar et al., 2023 ) . In contrast to these measures, humans naturally describe trajectories at a higher level, recognizing groups of strategies. Our key idea is to use LLMs as a higher-level interface for specifying differences through natural language, as humans do. This allows us to represent behaviors in terms of their high-level semantics rather than their low-level actions, providing a natural space for expressing diverse behaviors. We introduce PopGen , a framework that leverages LLMs to define semantically diverse behaviors in language space and translate them into executable policies that can interact with the environment. PopGen operates in two stages. First, it generates a diverse set of behavior descriptions in natural language, where high-level semantic differences can be expressed explicitly. We use tailored prompting methods to balance the quality of behavior descriptions with their semantic diversity, encouraging descriptions that are both meaningful and genuinely distinct. Second, PopGen grounds these high-level semantic descriptions into executable agent behaviors by synthesizing policy execution code. We generate the policy code in an iterative loop, where structured feedback from an advisor module guides progressive refinement. We use the diverse population generated by PopGen for population-play training and evaluate its impact on cooperation with novel partners. We find that training with semantically diverse partners improves robust cooperation, demonstrating the value of diverse behaviors. We further show that semantic diversity grows with larger PopGen populations, and that PopGen increases diversity while controlling for the quality of the synthetic agents ( Pugh et al., 2016 ) . Finally, we show that turning textual behavior descriptions into executable policy code, rather than LLM-generated reward functions, yields partners that more faithfully exhibit their specified behaviors and leads to more robust cooperators. In summary, our contributions are: • We propose PopGen , a framework that generates diverse agent populations from scratch by leveraging LLMs’ understanding of semantic diversity. • We show that training a cooperator against a PopGen population achieves the best performance across four collaborative environments when matched against other population-play baselines. • We provide extensive ablations that aim to understand the link between semantic diversity and downstream cooperation, as well as insights on methods to turn textual descriptions into executable agents using LLMs. 2 Related Work Generating diverse populations for ZSC. Zero-shot coordination requires a cooperator to work with teammates it never saw during training ( Hu et al., 2020 ) . Population play achieves this by training an agent against a set of partners, and how well population play works depends on the behavioral diversity of the population against which an agent is trained ( Bettini et al., 2024a ; McKee et al., 2022 ) . Existing methods for generating agent populations vary from pooling checkpoints across random seeds ( Strouse et al., 2021 ) to optimizing explicit diversity objectives over trajectory or action distributions ( Lupu et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , and more recently to sampling partners from a generative model of human play ( Liang et al., 2024 ) . These diversity measures all operate in trajectory, action, or latent space, where distances may not reflect the strategic distinctions a human would recognize ( Bettini et al., 2024c ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . We instead leverage the semantic diversity captured at the text level to generate diverse populations of agents. LLM-generated agents. LLMs can translate natural-language specifications into agents in several forms. LLM-as-Agent systems directly interact with the environment but require costly LLM calls during rollout ( Huang et al., 2022 ; Yao et al., 2023 ) , while reward-generation methods translate textual objectives into reward functions and train RL policies ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . However, designing rewards that faithfully capture high-level behaviors is challenging, as RL policies can optimize the reward without exhibiting the intended behavior ( Choi et al., 2025 ) . This challenge is pronounced in multi-agent settings, where interactions depend on other agents. Policy code instead provides a direct representation of behavior by explicitly encoding its decision logic ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Ahn et al., 2026 ) . Recent advances in LLM code generation further enable refining such policies through execution feedback ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Ahn et al., 2026 ) . In our experiments, we show that Policy Code more reliably realizes the specified behaviors than RL policies, resulting in higher behavioral adherence and stronger cooperator performance. 3 Problem Formulation Multi-agent interaction.
